mappings.note: Names what the aligned-holes set-up demonstrates, that light travels in a straight line: the property stated. The hands-on version of this is on LO-148.
The flame is lost in the bent pipe because light cannot follow the curve: the observation traced to its cause.
Names rectilinear propagation, the term for the straight-line property.
Names the transparent class.
Names the translucent class, the partial-transmission category.
Catches sunlight on a shiny plate, finds the spot on the wall and watches it move as the plate is tilted: an activity with recorded observations.
Sends a comb-slit beam along paper and then puts a mirror in its path: the reflection experiment as performed.
A shadow stays dark whatever the object's colour, because it is where light does not reach: the nature of shadows explained.
Tholu Bommalata and Ravana Chhaya as shadow play built on opaque cut-outs: the science behind a living cultural practice, so the application outcome.
Light changing direction at a shiny surface: the phenomenon stated.
Names reflection as that change of direction.
The beam's path changes at the mirror. Here the result is asked for as a fact about reflection rather than as an experiment to run, so LO-150 rather than LO-148.
What you see in a plane mirror is an image formed by reflected light.
Names the object as the real thing in front of the mirror: the vocabulary of image formation.
Matching item that pairs opaque with darker and translucent with lighter shadows (LO-146) and a larger shadow with the object being nearer the source (LO-149).
Matches Sun, Moon, opaque material and mirror image to luminous, non-luminous, light-blocking and virtual: category sorting throughout.
The Sun as the chief natural source of light.
Names the luminous category.
Names the non-luminous category.
Places the Moon in the non-luminous category.
Names the LED lamp as the low-power, long-life light source: identification of a device. The item about why LEDs are promoted is on C-SCI4.1.
Light travels in a straight line, the chapter's founding property.
Names the transparent category from how much light it passes.
Names the translucent category.
Names the opaque category.
Names the shadow as the dark patch behind a blocking object.
Defines the pinhole camera as a box in which light through a tiny hole forms an image: the device and its working.
The inverted image as the defining feature of that device.
Pinhole image inverted against mirror image erect: two kinds of image contrasted, which is about how each is formed. LO-146 covers materials and organisms, so it does not apply.
Whether the pinhole image carries colour: another property of the constructed device.
Sliding the inner box to sharpen the image: a design feature of the camera the class built.
Defines the periscope as two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped tube: the device and how it works.
Periscopes in submarines, tanks and bunkers: where the device is actually used, so the application outcome rather than its construction.
A shadow cast by red light is still dark, because a shadow is absence of light: the nature of shadows again, here against a coloured background.
Two angled mirrors give many images through repeated reflection: the phenomenon explained.
A small mirror can still image part of a large object, since the mirror limits the field of view rather than the image: image formation explained.
Light takes about eight minutes twenty seconds from the Sun: a fact about how light travels. Not LO-152, since the student measures or calculates nothing.
Assertion and reason tie shadow formation to straight-line travel: the explanation of both together.
Separates lateral inversion, which is true of mirror images, from being upside down, which is not: the properties of the image explained.
The tree seen in a pinhole camera as inverted and smaller: the image the device produces.
A written name appears left-right reversed in a mirror: lateral inversion as a property of the image.
Shadows are shortest near noon because the Sun is then highest: the daily pattern tied to its cause.
Lateral inversion plus the symmetry of letters such as T and O: both statements concern how the mirror image is formed.
Where the two mirrors must sit in a Z-tube periscope, at forty-five degrees and parallel: the design of the device.

A distant bird's shadow spreads and fades before it reaches the ground: the visibility traced to the object-to-screen distance. Note that the printed key marks option D while the explanation supports B, which is reported as a defect.
